A finite tensor theorem excludes those identities.

outputs.exact_statement: There is a finitely presented group $G$ with a finite, oriented, four-dimensional aspherical Poincaré complex $Q$ such that $$H^i(G;\mathbb ZG)=0\quad(i\ne4),\qquad H^4(G;\mathbb ZG)\cong\mathbb Z$$ with trivial right $G$-action on the last group, but no closed aspherical topological four-manifold has fundamental group $G$. In particular the trivial left $\mathbb ZG$-module $\mathbb Z$ has a finite resolution by finitely generated free modules.

There are a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold $D$, its connected boundary $S$, a finitely generated free group $H$, and a map $c:D\to BH$ with the following properties.*

1.  *The map $c$ induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups, and $D$ has the homotopy type of a finite graph with $2k$ two-spheres attached at its basepoint. Its module $\pi_2D$ has a specified hyperbolic basis over $\mathbb ZH$, represented by framed immersed spheres with vanishing quadratic self-intersection obstructions.*

2.  *Attach a three-cell to each basis sphere, and denote the resulting space by $P$. Then $(P,S)$ is an oriented Poincaré pair of formal dimension four, and $P\simeq BH$. The boundary marking is $c|_S:S\to BH$.*

3.  *There is no compact oriented topological four-manifold $D'$ with boundary identified with $S$ and a homotopy equivalence $c':D'\to BH$ whose restriction to $S$ is homotopic to $c|_S$.

With the surface-product trivializations, the exterior and its tube-side maps have the homotopy-pushout model $$E\simeq X\cup_{\coprod_jF_j}\coprod_j(F_j\times S^1),$$ where each gluing map to $F_j\times S^1$ is the inward section. The displayed $F_j\times S^1$ maps represent the actual tube sides.
The map $\pi_1S\to H$ is onto. If $r=\operatorname{rank}H$, then $H_1(S;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(P;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism and $H_2(S;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$.

Let $V$ be one of the filled compact vertex pieces and let $Z$ be its finite set of punctures. In degree zero take smooth functions on $V\setminus Z$ separately constant near each puncture, and in positive degrees take smooth forms vanishing near the punctures. This differential graded algebra computes $H^*(V;\mathbb C)$, naturally on the unpunctured faces. It supports the vertex calculation in the Vertex data Proposition of [[TO](#ref-TO)], with the filled cohomology groups and with the same Stokes identities.

Put $Y=\mathcal U(C,D)$ and let $D_c$ be its chamber with label $c$. Order $C$ by nondecreasing word length, breaking ties arbitrarily. Every finite initial segment containing the identity is, after rounding its collar corners, an iterated boundary connected sum of its chambers. In particular $$U_L=\bigcup_{|c|\leq L}D_c$$ is a compact manifold with boundary the connected sum of the corresponding copies of $S$. Its fundamental group is the free product of their chamber groups. The same statements hold if any chambers have been stabilized in their interiors.
The group $\widehat C\rtimes H$, and hence its finite-index subgroup $G$, acts properly and cocompactly by isometries on a proper CAT(0) cube complex of dimension at most five.

There is a $C$-equivariant continuous map $$\eta:Y\longrightarrow\Sigma_C$$ which sends the inner core of each chamber to its label, respects the panels, and has uniformly bounded image diameter on each chamber. On the boundary collar of the central chamber its radial directions at the identity vertex give the dual-block identification with $S$. After interior chamber stabilizations, the same construction gives a continuous map with the same panel, core, and diameter properties; it is equivariant under any subgroup preserving the stabilized pattern.

With the identifications above, $$\label{st:fundamental-equality}
 (u_N)_*[N]=(u_L)_*[L]\quad\text{in }H_4(B;\mathbb Z).$$
There is an orientation-preserving homotopy equivalence $$f\colon N\longrightarrow L$$ inducing the specified isomorphism on $\pi_1$ and the prescribed isometry $A\to\pi_2(L)$.
There is an $s$-cobordism $(W;N,L)$ whose two end inclusions identify $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ by the marking of Proposition 12.

For some integer $k\ge0$ there is a homeomorphism $$h\colon N\mathbin{\#}\,k(S^2\times S^2)
 \longrightarrow
 L\mathbin{\#}\,k(S^2\times S^2)$$ which induces the prescribed original marking and matches every added standard pair with its specified added standard pair. In particular, on the left, all the prescribed original hyperbolic pairs and all new standard pairs have simultaneous geometric representatives with pairwise disjoint punctured $S^2\times S^2$ neighborhoods.

The manifold $Y$ has two $\Delta$-periodic systems of sphere pairs, with the same chamber labels:*

1.  *framed immersed hyperbolic pairs in the interiors of the chambers $D_v$, including the added standard pairs, with their equivariant products already correct over the individual chamber group;*

2.  *geometrically standard pairs with pairwise disjoint punctured $S^2\times S^2$ neighborhoods, based-homotopic sphere by sphere to the correspondingly labelled pairs in the first system.*

*There is an integer $d_0$ such that the drawing of each pair, its standard neighborhood, and the homotopies relating the two systems are contained in the chambers at gallery distance at most $d_0$ from that pair’s label. Basings in this statement are local basings transported with the chamber; no bound is asserted for whiskers drawn from one global base point to all chambers.

For every such stabilized chamber there is a simply connected compact oriented topological four-manifold $J$ with boundary $-S$ such that $$H_2(S;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_2(J;\mathbb Z)
 \quad\text{is an isomorphism},\qquad H_3(J;\mathbb Z)=0.$$ Moreover, $D\cup_S J$ is simply connected, and inclusion of $D$ identifies its second homology and intersection form with those of $D\cup_S J$.

Fix a positive integer $h$. In $Y_R$, the projected pairs of $\mathcal A$ labelled by $|v|>R$ admit the following preparation, with propagation bounded independently of $R$:*

1.  *The two halves are represented by framed immersed spheres $a_i,b_i$ with $a_i\cap b_j$ consisting of the designated single point for $i=j$ and empty for $i\ne j$.*

2.  *The remaining intersections among the $a_i$ are paired by framed Whitney discs. Each Whitney disc is replaced by a properly immersed capped grope of height at least $h$ with the same framed attaching region.*

3.  *These gropes have the Clifford dual capped surfaces used in [[PRT](#ref-PRT), Definition 3.1 and Lemma 4.1]. In particular, their caps miss the *entire* dual capped surfaces, and the bodies of the latter lie in a boundary collar of the complement of the $a_i$.*

*The construction uses no complementary filling $J_v$. Beyond a fixed gallery distance from the peeling region, it can be carried out separately inside individual chambers.

Fix a propagation bound $b$. For objects carried within $b$ galleries of labels $v$ with $|v|\to\infty$, their direction images in $S$ have diameter tending uniformly to zero. This assertion continues to hold after peeling for the whole region of bounded propagation around the outer systems, if $R$ is sufficiently large.*

*Let $\beta:S\to BH$ be the central boundary marking. On that region, the homomorphism induced by the direction map followed by $\beta$ agrees, up to the common change of base path, with inclusion into $Z$ followed by its classifying map. In particular, every loop in an image system whose entire direction image lies in a contractible patch of $S$ is nullhomotopic in $Z$.

Suppose a finite prepared Whitney-grope system as in Lemma 17 has at least eight surface stages. Retain its first five stages. Suppose the upper capped subgropes, of height at least three, have uniformly small direction images in the region of Lemma 18. If their diameters are sufficiently small, depending only on a fixed finite coordinate cover of $S$, the upper subgropes can be replaced by mutually disjoint framed immersed cap discs. Their self-intersection loops are nullhomotopic in $Z$. The retained stages and the entire protected Clifford capped surfaces remain unchanged.

The compact manifold $Z$ admits interior surgeries producing a compact oriented topological four-manifold $V$ with boundary $S$, fundamental group $H$, and contractible universal cover. The boundary map to $BH$ is the original central marking.

outputs.exact_statement: There exist finite connected graphs $(X_j)_{j\geq1}$ with a common finite bound on vertex degree, a coarse disjoint union $X=\bigsqcup_{j\geq1}X_j$, and an infinite-order class $\alpha\in\mathop{\mathrm{KX}}_1(X)$ such that $$\mu_X^{\max}(\alpha)=0.$$ Consequently, $\mu_X^{\max}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is not injective.

The maps $Q_{k+1}\to Q_k$ are surjective and have kernels of size at most $2^9$. For every fixed word radius $R$, the reduction $\Gamma\to Q_k$ is injective on the $S$-word ball of radius $R$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

The graphs $B_j,Y_j,X_j$ are finite and connected, with vertex degrees bounded independently of $j$. Their projections to $B_j$ are $1$-Lipschitz. Each end copy of $B_j$ is isometrically embedded in $X_j$.

If $l_j>4r$, there is a continuous map $$p_{B,j}:P_r(B_j)\longrightarrow T_j$$ whose restriction to $T_j\subseteq P_3(B_j)\subseteq P_r(B_j)$ is the identity. The graph projections define continuous maps $$p_{Y,j}:P_r(Y_j)\longrightarrow T_j,
 \qquad
 p_{X,j}:P_r(X_j)\longrightarrow T_j$$ by composition with $p_{B,j}$.

For every fixed integer $r\geq3$ and all sufficiently large $j$, $$p_{Y,j}^*(u_1\smile u_2)
 \in 2^j H^2(P_r(Y_j);\mathbb Z).
 \label{top:chern-divisibility-eq}$$ Equivalently, there is a line bundle $\mathcal L'_{j,r}$ on $P_r(Y_j)$ such that $$p_{Y,j}^*\mathcal L_j
 \cong(\mathcal L'_{j,r})^{\otimes 2^j}.
 \label{top:line-root}$$

For every fixed integer $r\geq3$ and all sufficiently large $j$, $$p_{Y,j}^*\theta_j\in
 2^{\,j-\lfloor\log_2D_r\rfloor}K^1(P_r(Y_j)).
 \label{top:k-divisibility-eq}$$

Fix an integer $r\geq3$ and a nonzero integer $n$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $$n(t_{+,j,r})_*\tau_j-n(t_{-,j,r})_*\tau_j
 \neq0\quad\text{in }K_1(P_r(X_j)).
 \label{top:component-nonzero}$$
The class $\alpha\in\mathop{\mathrm{KX}}_1(X)$ defined in [top:alpha] has infinite order. In particular, $\alpha\otimes1\neq0$ in $\mathop{\mathrm{KX}}_1(X)\otimes\mathbb Q$.

An operator in $\mathbb C[Z]$ supported on $F\times F$, for a finite set $F\subset Z$, has the same maximal and concrete norms. The closure in $A_Z$ of all such operators is an ideal $\mathcal K_Z$, canonically isomorphic to $\mathcal K(H_Z)$. In particular, $K_1(\mathcal K_Z)=0$.

Conjugation by an exact covering isometry defines a $*$-homomorphism $$h_A=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}(V_h):A_Z\longrightarrow A_W.$$ Its induced map on $K$-theory is independent of the covering isometry. These induced maps respect composition, and an exact covering isometry over $\mathop{\mathrm{id}}_Z$ induces the identity on $K_*(A_Z)$.

For the classes $\beta\in\mathop{\mathrm{KX}}_1(B)$ and $\alpha=(i_+)_*\beta-(i_-)_*\beta\in\mathop{\mathrm{KX}}_1(X)$ constructed above, $$\label{eq:ana-naturality}
 \mu_X^{\max}(\alpha)
 =(i_{+,A})_*\mu_B^{\max}(\beta)
  -(i_{-,A})_*\mu_B^{\max}(\beta).$$

For the projection $f:Y\to B$ there is a $*$-homomorphism $$\Phi:A_B\longrightarrow A_Y$$ such that $(f_A\Phi)_*=\mathop{\mathrm{id}}$ on $K_*(A_B)$. In particular, $$(f_A)_*:K_1(A_Y)\longrightarrow K_1(A_B)$$ is surjective.

For $T\in\mathbb C[B]$, the operator $L(T)$ belongs to $\mathbb C[Y]$ and commutes with $P$. For $T,T'\in\mathbb C[B]$, the defect $$\label{eq:transport-defect}
 D=L(T)L(T')-L(TT')$$ has finite vertex support and satisfies $PD=0$ in $A_Y$.

The endpoint maps induce the same homomorphism $$(i_{+,A}f_A)_*=(i_{-,A}f_A)_*:
 K_1(A_Y)\longrightarrow K_1(A_X).$$
